summary: A status report saying the UCSB remote job entry and output retrieval services described in RFC 105 had been used successfully from Rand. Rand users reached them through a network service program on video-graphic consoles, and one Rand research group had started using the facility for real work. It is an early report of a working ARPANET service.

eli5.summary: Two faraway schools tried a new mail-in homework service. This note says it works, and some students are already using it for real work.

questions: did the ucsb remote job entry service work from rand
what was the network service program at rand
how fast was early arpanet file transfer
subtitle: A 1971 field report on using UCSB's remote job service from Rand, with timings and a few failures.

tldr.problem: The network's early users needed to know whether remote job submission over the network actually worked in practice.
tldr.mechanism: Rand reports on running jobs at UCSB through its Network Service Program, giving typical job sizes, a transmission timing study and a list of observed failures.
tldr.outcome: The service worked and was used in production on a limited basis, but transfer was slow at about 250 cards per minute and a few messages failed for unknown reasons.

today: RFC 113 is a 1971 status report, not a specification; it was updated by RFC 227.

sections.title: UCSB RJE/RJOR From Rand
sections.content:
The UCSB Remote Job Entry (RJE) and Remote Job Output Retrieval (RJOR) systems, described in RFC 105, were used and validated from Rand. Another research group at Rand was by then using the facility on a limited basis as a production tool.

Rand reached UCSB through its Network Service Program (NSP), driven by Rand Video-Graphic consoles. A small module, UCSBMGR, was added to NSP to handle the RJE and RJOR protocols and data formats. Typical jobs were input decks of 800 to 2800 80-character card images and output files of about 30 pages of printer listings.
sections.eli5: Rand's computer learned how to send big stacks of work to a computer at UCSB and get the printed answers back.

sections.title: Speed of Transfer
sections.content:
A timing study of a 2800 record file showed an average rate of 250 80-character cards per minute, with each card sent as a separate network message. The authors note this is much less than the advertised 30 kilobit rate, although the path from Rand to UCSB passes through at least one intermediate IMP.

The processes at each end ran at maximum priority with very small loads, so the slowness was not due to busy machines. The authors suggest blocking card images together for transmission as an obvious area for speed-up.
sections.eli5: Sending each card as its own little package was slow, like mailing every page of a book in its own envelope. Putting pages together would be faster.

sections.title: Failures Observed
sections.content:
Over about two months the authors saw approximately five serious failures. In two cases the RFNM on the control link from UCSB to Rand was lost, and the loss was not reported by a type 9 IMP-to-Host message as expected. They could not reproduce it, so they could not tell whether the IMP or the UCSB host interface was at fault.

The other three were garbled data messages, each time the second card image sent to RJE. The HASP system at UCSB ignored the image instead of printing it, so the cause stayed unknown. This problem appeared in early transmissions and then disappeared. The authors were fairly confident their own host software was not at fault, and note that over 100 jobs had been run at UCSB from Rand.
sections.eli5: A few times a message got lost or scrambled and nobody could work out why. But over a hundred jobs went through fine.

references.text: NWG/RFC #105, describing the UCSB RJE and RJOR systems.
